articles.title_orig: China touts AI milestone: models generate more tokens than used in training
articles.title_zh: China touts AI milestone: models generate more tokens than used in training
articles.content_orig:
Average daily token calls exceed 175 trillion, government-backed report says, indicating growing demand for AI services
For the first time, the amount of inference data generated by artificial intelligence systems in China has surpassed the amount of data used to train those systems, according to a new government-backed report, illustrating how the country is increasingly adopting AI at scale.
The report released on Saturday by the China Centre for Information Industry Development (CCID), which operates under China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), cited recent official data showing that China’s average daily token calls exceeded 175 trillion, an increase of more than 1,000 times from early 2024.
Inference refers to the process of running trained AI models to respond to user requests, which involves processing units of data known as tokens. As AI adoption accelerates, the volume of token calls, which refers to AI usage through public cloud service providers, provides an indication of growing demand for AI services.

articles.title_orig: Oil prices fall amid reports that the U.S. and Iran are both seeking diplomacy
articles.title_zh: Oil prices fall amid reports that the U.S. and Iran are both seeking diplomacy
articles.content_orig:
Oil fell Monday amid news that both the U.S. and Iran seek diplomatic options to their conflict.
Futures for international benchmark Brent crude for January delivery fell 3.31% to $109.67 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for December declined 3.34% to $100.64 per barrel.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that President Donald Trump prefers not to use military force and would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically."
Trump "hasn't made a decision...what the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it, and we really we have everything we need to be successful. But we would prefer to do it peacefully," Rubio said, speaking to reporters over the weekend.
Iranian authorities also signaled that a deal is still possible, following two days of talks mediated by Qatar, as long as demands are implemented tangibly, according to Al Jazeera.
The news come following reports that both the U.S. and Iran are preparing for more military strikes after the midterm elections.
Reports from The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times indicate that the U.S. is preparing for possible renewed military actions after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Saturday called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
Concerns over the Middle East and Ukraine conflicts will likely linger in the near term.
"Attacks on ships and refineries in the Middle East and on civilians in Ukraine continue, doing little to inspire confidence in the prospects for lasting ceasefires in the foreseeable future," said Tamas Varga, analyst at PVM Oil Associates.
"Nonetheless, hope springs eternal," Varga added.
—CNBC's Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: UK making up China policy ‘as it goes along’, MPs warn
articles.title_zh: UK making up China policy ‘as it goes along’, MPs warn
articles.content_orig:
Commons committee says lack of coherent strategy is hampering business and leaving national security risks unaddressed
The UK is making up policy on China “as it goes along” and risks having its strategy dictated by Washington or Beijing, a parliamentary report has concluded.
An investigation by the Commons business, innovation, science and trade select committee said Labour’s failure to formulate a coherent strategy since 2024 “combined the worst of both worlds” for the UK in relation to China.
Liam Byrne, Labour MP and chair of the committee said the UK’s policy on China meant it was also endangering its business with the EU with the risk of being “cut off” from big manufacuring contracts.
The government could neither deliver commercial opportunities to British businesses nor control the “increasing exposure to unquantified, managed risk” in relations with China, it found.
The report said: “In 2024, the new government promised a strategic, long-term, consistent UK approach to China. It has not delivered on this.
“Britain must shape its own relationship with China or risk having that relationship shaped for us in Washington or Beijing.”
The UK’s relationship with China has been marked by a lack of engagement in the last 10 years, with Keir Starmer making the first official visit in January since Theresa May in 2018.
That trip was billed as an effort to end the “diplomatic ice age”, but since 2018 China has benefited from an export boom that is now fuelling fears about deindustrialisation, adding to deep-seated existing concerns about cyber espionage and national security.
The MPs acknowledged the advantages of trading with Beijing in their report, noting that British businesses have profitable operations in China and “are ambitious to grow” and learn from the country’s “world-leading” innovations.
At the same time, consumers benefit from low-cost imports when household incomes are squeezed, with electric vehicles being a case in point.
However, Byrne sharply criticised the government’s piecemeal approach.
“Britain’s businesses cannot plan for the future when the government keeps making up its China policy as it goes along.
“Ministers promised clarity and consistency. Instead, we have opportunities missed, risks unmanaged and decisions left until the 11th hour.”
The committee cited the decision in March to block the Chinese firm Ming Yang from building a £1.5bn wind energy plant in Scotland after years of negotiation because of unspecified security risks.
Scotland’s first minister, John Swinney, has called on Andy Burnham to reconsider Starmer’s decision.
That decision, along with the emergency takeover of British Steel from its Chinese owners, “has been characterised by reactivity, inconsistency and opacity”, the report said.
Work on a new strategy, the committee said, should be combined with official preparations for new trade remedies to counter unfair competition, including potential tariffs on EVs, something Downing Street has not ruled out.
The report calls for “clear new rules of the game” and recommends the designation of a “red zone” for industries that would be off-limits for Chinese investment and a “green zone”, where trade should be encouraged.
Byrne said a China strategy was an urgent concern as “Europe is changing fast” and “proposing new trade protections as it gets bolder with Beijing and warier of Washington”.
The new laws “may trap Britain outside EU trade walls, cutting us off from our largest market”.
Byrne said the government “should be prepared to consider dynamic alignment” with the EU include tariffs on EVs “as the price of securing British firms a place in the EU’s Made in Europe project” and to help guard against China dominance.
The UK is already under pressure to align with the EU on tariffs on EVs, but the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, has said he will make a decision in the best interests of the UK.
The EU has already imposed tariffs on Chinese EVs, capped the number of hybrid cars that can be imported from China and is now considering a Franco-German proposal for a “kill switch” to block imports if China weaponises trade – as it did last year with curbs on exports of rare-earth minerals and chips. “The UK’s partners are moving further and faster,” the report noted.
China is now on track to surpass last year’s record $1.19tn trade surplus with the rest of the world.
Its latest five-year plan, covering 2026 to 2030, gives a glimpse of where China is going next in prioritising the strategic expansion of high-value green exports such as EVs, batteries, wind turbines, hydrogen and solar panels.

articles.title_orig: Russia and Ukraine say emergency alert apps were hit by apparent cyber-attacks
articles.title_zh: Russia and Ukraine say emergency alert apps were hit by apparent cyber-attacks
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine and Russia say their emergency warning apps have been hit by cyber-attacks, causing false alerts to be issued
Moscow says a "massive cyber-attack" has affected its app but insists its wider alert system is "operating as normal" . A Ukrainian espionage group claims the messages included fake warnings of nuclear strikes inside Russia
This comes shortly after Ukraine's air raid warning app sent out false warnings of a radiation threat in Kyiv , following an apparent hack
Ukraine has blamed Russia for the hack on its app, while Moscow is yet to say who it believes is behind the cyber-attack on its system
The alerts in Ukraine were sent out just minutes before the end of a localised ceasefire in the front-line Kherson region, our Ukraine reporter Abdujalil Abdurasulov writes
Edited by Toby Mann and Yvette Tan
While we wait for further information on the apparent cyber attacks in Russia and Ukraine, here's the latest on the strikes that were reported overnight.
In a statement on Telegram, Russia's Ministry of Defence says it struck a Ukrainian military cargo vessel at sea 58km south of Odesa overnight.
It says the vessel was "delivering cargo intended for the Ukrainian Armed Forces".
Another strike hit a storage site for Ukrainian missile launch systems in the Odesa village of Tuzly, it says.
Meanwhile, a Telegram channel for the city of Odesa says four people were injured in strikes in Odesa overnight. "All received prompt medical assistance," the update says.
It adds that two private homes, a garage and city infrastructure also sustained "significant damage".
The false alerts started at approximately 22:47 (20:47 GMT) on Sunday, with red-level air raids apparently issued nationwide, in Ukrainian.
Additional warnings were issued in Kyiv, with the first reading: "Radiation threat. Radiation threat declared in Kyiv."
The next message, written in Russian, came at 22:48 , which read: "Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don't worry, it's Oreshnik flying". Oreshnik is the name of a Russian intermediate-range ballistic missile capable of carrying nuclear or conventional warheads.
A third alert, at 22:49 , again in Ukrainian, said "Chemical threat. There is a threat of a chemical attack on Kyiv. Don't go outside."
At 22:49 , a fourth alert stated there was a "street fighting threat. Street fighting is taking place in Kyiv. Don't go outside."
At 23:53 a series of all clear messages were then delivered to users' phones, which were connected to each of the previous Kyiv alerts, individually declaring each threat clear.
We don't know much about the alerts sent out in Russia. But as we reported earlier, a Ukrainian espionage group claimed fake warnings of nuclear strikes inside Russia had been sent to users.
Dan Johnson Ukraine correspondent, reporting from Kyiv
Ukraineâs air raid alert app usually warns of incoming Russian drones or missiles.
Last night it issued alerts of a radiological threat, a chemical attack and street fighting here in Kyiv.
The warnings were followed by all clear messages just over an hour later.
The air force issued a statement saying the app had been hacked and reassured citizens there was no imminent threat of nuclear war, blaming Russian interference.
Hours later, Russiaâs emergencies ministry claimed it had also suffered a cyber attack and said people were receiving emails containing fake information.
Itâs not clear if the two incidents are connected.
Oleksander Merezhko, chair of the Ukrainian parliament's foreign affairs committee, has told the BBC the attack did not cause panic or extreme reactions.
Merezhko says Ukrainians, especially in Kyiv, are used to "practically non-stop alerts".
"Secondly, this message was in Russian language which immediately aroused suspicions," he says.
"It's a very unpleasant fact but it is part of cyber war and people in Ukraine understand that. It is possible and we are quite prepared for such possibilities," adds Merezhko, a member of President Volodymyr Zelensky's Servant of the People party,
Russia and Ukraine both say their emergency alert systems have been hit by cyber-attacks. Here's what we know so far:
The BBC's Newsday programme has just spoken to Herbert Lin, a senior research scholar for cyber policy and security at Stanford University, who describes the hacking of Ukraine's air strike alert system as "concerning".
âI think itâs the first time itâs happened to an official Ukrainian information app, but I suspect it wonât be the last,â says Lin, who previously served on former US President Barack Obamaâs Commission on Enhancing National Cybersecurity.
âWe donât know how they did it yetâ¦ Maybe in the future theyâll be able to do it more but we just donât know yet.â
Russia and Ukraine have also exchanged strikes targeting each other's energy infrastructure.
Russia said drone strikes hit an "industrial enterprise" east of Moscow overnight, which Ukrainian media identified as the Kstovo oil refinery.
The governor of Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region - home to the Kstovo plant - described a "massive" drone attack during the night and morning.
Gleb Nikitin said significant damage was sustained and warned of power outages and reduced hot water supplies. He said one woman was injured as a result of falling drone debris.
Ukrainian forces have repeatedly attacked Russian oil and gas sites in retaliation for Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had struck energy infrastructure in four regions overnight on Saturday, leaving hundreds of thousands of homes without power. A Reuters report quoted him as saying the intensity of these strikes were "very high".
Some connections were restored on Sunday.

The fake alert sent to Russia's emergency app had warned users that "nuclear warheads mounted on P1-Suns [a Ukrainian attack drone] had been launched at all regions of Russia".
The alert, which opened with a message telling residents there was a "risk of getting lively" also told them to "stock up urgently on food for three weeks and hide".
Emergency alert apps in Ukraine and Russia have been hacked, according to reports.
The Ukraine government's Center for Strategic Communications has blamed Russia for the hack in a post on its X account, saying one of the alerts was a "message in Russian about Oreshnik".
A few hours later, Moscow also said that its emergency alert app had been hit by a "massive cyber-attack" - but did not immediately say who might be behind it.
Ukraine's Centre for Strategic Communications has blamed Russia for the hack in a post on its X account.
It posted a picture showing some of the alerts that had showed up on Ukraine's air raid warning app and asked residents to "disregard" any "strange messages" they might see in the app.
The Russian emergencies ministry says its public alert system is "operating as normal", stressing that citizens are informed of alerts through multiple channels including sirens and loudspeakers, text messages, and TV and radio broadcasts, and that the app is "only an additional, ancillary news service".
"The hacking of the mobile app has not had, and cannot have, any impact on the operation of the public alert system," it said on its Telegram channel.
It said specialists were working to restore normal operation of the mobile app but the situation was "under control".

articles.title_zh: Police with assault rifles begin Sydney patrols in wake of Bondi attack
articles.content_orig:
A new police unit armed with military assault rifles has begun patrolling the streets of Sydney, in an Australian-first measure set up in response to the Bondi Beach attack last December.
The Armed Response Command will deploy at major events, crowded public spaces, sporting venues, and places of worship to conduct "high visibility" patrols, New South Wales state police said. The A$94 million ($66.08 million) unit is composed of 250 police officers armed with Australian combat assault rifles.
The measure is the first of its kind in Australia , where the presence of heavily armed police officers is rare.
"The tragic events at Bondi demonstrated the devastating consequences when an alleged armed offender attacks innocent people," the unit's commander, Detective Superintendent Andrew Evans, said.
"ARC ensures we have highly trained officers in the right places, with the right equipment, ready to act when seconds matter."
Amnesty International Australia said the introduction of heavily armed police patrols in Sydney raised "serious questions about the increasing militarisation of policing and the safeguards in place to protect human rights.

articles.title_orig: Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, November 1, 2026
articles.title_zh: Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, November 1, 2026
articles.source: Institute for the Study of War
articles.content_orig:
Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment
Russian forces lost ground on the battlefield in October 2026 for the second month in a row. ISW has observed evidence to assess that Russian forces consolidated positions or seized 139.85 kilometers but lost 167.14 square kilometers of territory in Ukraine in October 2026 for a net loss of 27.29 square kilometers. That is an average pace of -0.88 square kilometers per day. Russian forces only made gains in Sumy and Zaporizhia oblasts, while losing territory in all other sectors of the frontline, including their priority objective of Donetsk Oblast. Russian forces also lost ground in October when accounting for Russian infiltrations into areas over which Russian forces have not gained control, with Russian forces suffering a net loss of 76.38 square kilometers in such areas for an average pace of -2.46 square kilometers per day. Russian forces seized 10 settlements totaling 5.86 square kilometers, but Ukrainian forces liberated or cleared Russian infiltrators from 11 settlements with an area of 3.24 square kilometers.
Russian forces suffered their highest monthly losses of the war thus far in October 2026, paying a growing price for their territorial losses. The Ukrainian General Staff reported that Russian forces lost 54,400 killed or seriously wounded in October 2026 — the fourth consecutive month that Russian forces suffered over 40,000 monthly casualties and Russia’s highest monthly casualty total since the Kremlin launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.[1] Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) Commander Major Robert “Magyar” Brovdi noted that Russian forces suffered the highest losses in the Dobropillya, Oleksandrivka, and Hulyaipole directions.[2] Russian forces continue to sustain significant personnel losses while losing ground, and Russia’s current force generation system continues to recruit fewer soldiers than needed to replace these losses.[3] These factors likely explain Russian President Vladimir Putin’s turn to a new theory of victory that relies on using long-range ballistic missiles and jet-powered drone strikes to hammer Ukraine into surrender over the winter.
Russian casualty rates and territorial losses match the battlefield reality that Russian forces have lost the initiative and their offensive capabilities in much of the theater. Russian forces retain the initiative in the immediate area of Dobropillya, Donetsk Oblast, where they have concentrated the bulk of their offensive operations. But Ukrainian forces have seized the initiative in the Kupyansk, Lyman, and Oleksandrivka directions and are contesting it in western Zaporizhia Oblast.
Russian forces have managed to make marginal advances in the Dobropillya direction by committing substantial resources and personnel, but the seizure of Dobropillya would not enable sweeping Russian advances in Donetsk Oblast. Russian forces attacking toward Dobropillya are part of a broader Russian effort intended to form the southern part of the wide encirclement of the Fortress Belt together with Russian offensive operations north of Lyman.[4] The Russian military command has committed significant resources and personnel to achieving its objective of seizing Dobropillya, including deploying most of the Russian 41st Combined Arms Army (CAA, Central Military District [CMD]) to reinforce Russian elements attacking just northeast of Dobropillya and east of the Kazenyi Torets River, and deploying roughly one-third of Russia’s elite Rubikon Center for Advanced Unmanned Systems forces to the Dobropillya direction.[5] Ukrainian General Staff offensive intensity data indicates that Russian forces have consistently maintained their highest offensive tempo on the frontline in the Pokrovsk (south of Dobropillya) direction. Russian forces have concentrated their attacks in that area on Dobropillya and its immediate environs, averaging roughly 30 attacks per day through November 1, and this direction has been the highest-intensity sector since at least August 1, 2026.[6] Russian forces have maintained intensified offensive operations toward Dobropillya instead of reallocating resources to attack toward Druzhkivka, which could produce more tangible successes. Russian forces have recently made limited gains toward Dobropillya, primarily in the form of small-group infiltration missions, but have not consolidated any positions in the town.[7] Russian forces’ high offensive tempo has not translated into meaningful gains in the Dobropillya direction that will enable Russian forces to achieve their objective of seizing the Fortress Belt by Spring 2027 — the most recent of many deadlines that Putin has given the Russian military.[8]
Russian forces’ continued intensified operations toward Dobropillya likely reflect the Russian military command’s delusional belief that it will be able to restore operational maneuver on the battlefield. A Russian seizure of Dobropillya would not enable Russia to make sweeping advances in Donetsk Oblast, however. The Russian military command originally intended to use Dobropillya as the western anchor of a wide encirclement of the Fortress Belt meant to meet Russian forces that were supposed to advance on the northern flank of the Fortress Belt through Lyman to eventually meet up in Barvinkove, Kharkiv Oblast.[9] Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi in the Lyman direction has defeated Russian forces’ attempt to develop the northern pincer, rendering the possible seizure of Dobropillya meaningless within the framework of the original campaign plan since that plan is no longer feasible.[10] The Russian command has shown no indication that it has changed its original campaign plan to account for the defeat east of Lyman, but it could conceivably hope to use a drive north from Dobropillya to cut Ukrainian ground lines of communication (GLOCs) to Kramatorsk and the rest of the fortress belt cities. Russian forces have shown none of the capabilities that would be necessary to undertake such an operation, however, as they remain unable to conduct rapid operational maneuver. An operation to seize Dobropillya and then subsequently launch an offensive against Kramatorsk from the west would require enormous quantities of manpower and resources and take years, if it is possible at all.
The Russian military command does not appear to have modified plans even for the forces defeated by Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi in the Lyman direction. Operation Vivaldi collapsed the Russian salient north and northwest of Lyman that was intended to be the base of the northern pincer of the Russian encirclement of the Fortress Belt. Ukrainian counterattacks have both denied Russian forces the opportunity to conduct a wide encirclement of the Fortress Belt from the north and blocked Russian plans for enveloping Slovyansk itself from the northeast. The Russian military command nonetheless appears committed to its original campaign design even in this sector. Ukrainian General Staff reports indicate that Russian forces averaged around 7.4 attacks per day in the Lyman direction in October 2026 — down only slightly from their September average of 8.4 attacks per day.[11] The Russian military command has also redeployed elements of the Russian 1st Guards Tank Army (GTA, Moscow Military District [MMD]) from the Kupyansk direction to the Lyman direction to support offensive operations, as Ukrainian counterattacks significantly degraded the Russian 20th CAA (MMD) and 25th CAA (CMD).[12] The movement of this reinforcement to the Lyman area may have been intended in part to stabilize the Russian lines in the face of continuing Ukrainian counteroffensive operations, but Russian forces continue seeking to advance in this area and are not merely focused on stabilizing their lines.

articles.title_orig: I moved to Thailand for a slower life. Over a year into retirement, I missed having a purpose.
articles.title_zh: I moved to Thailand for a slower life. Over a year into retirement, I missed having a purpose.
articles.content_orig:
This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Michael Kane, 54, who moved to Koh Samui, Thailand, to retire. It has been edited for length and clarity.
I grew up in Orange County, Southern California, and started my career in restaurants before getting into software. Over the years, I worked in many different fields, from construction and real estate to sales and marketing.
I moved to Atlanta in 1990 and lived there for most of the next 30 years.
About a decade ago, a friend invited me to Thailand for a couple of weeks. I liked the place so much that I stayed for three months. After that, I began splitting my time between Thailand and the US.
My last business before leaving the US was a doggy day care outside Atlanta, which I started after struggling to find one nearby for my own dog. The pandemic hit just before it opened, but I was thankfully able to sell it. After that, I decided I was done with running businesses in the US.
For a long time, I knew I did not want to spend the rest of my life in the US. I had traveled internationally for much of my career, and I felt that spending the rest of my life appreciating other cultures, specifically Thai culture, seemed more appealing.
So, in 2020, I moved to Koh Samui , an island in Thailand, to retire. I bought a two-bedroom apartment in Mae Nam, in the northern area of the island, for $186,100.
I initially came on a five-year Thailand Elite visa, which has since been restructured into the Thailand Privilege visa.
When the Thai government announced the Long-Term Resident Wealthy Pensioners visa in 2022, I decided to switch to that instead, since it was valid for 10 years.
Create a BI Job Scout and get opportunities matched to your goals.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
When I moved to Koh Samui , I was looking for a slower life.
I spent my first year and a half there doing what people imagine retirement on a Thai island looks like: going to the beach, getting massages, and enjoying the freedom of not having to work.
But there are only so many days you can spend at the beach and so many massages you can get. I started to get bored.
I don't play golf, I don't fish, I don't paint, and I don't write poetry.
My ex-girlfriend, a personal trainer , was making banana cakes in our kitchen and selling them around the island. I suggested renting a small space so we could put in ovens and turn it into a little business.
I also couldn't find good coffee on the island, and we thought it would go well with the cakes. I started researching it and got really immersed, which eventually led us to open Izzy’s Coffee. We named it after my dog.
It started as a small outdoor kiosk that cost about 100,000 Thai baht to build. We then spent another 400,000 Thai baht on equipment and furnishings.
Being on the Long-Term Resident visa allowed me to get a work permit. My current partner, Yam, and I now run the café together. I developed all our drinks.
About six months ago, we questioned why we were standing outside in the heat, rain, and noise. We decided to enclose the kiosk and turned it into a café.
I'm around every day, talking to people and making sure every customer has a perfect experience.
Thailand is not the panacea people think it is. It can be expensive and challenging to live here legally. But I have built a life here, and I am pretty happy.
I have only been back to the US once in the six years I have lived here — it was for a funeral.
But moving to Thailand has not meant losing touch with the people I care about. Even after our divorce, my ex-wife and I have remained close. She and her new husband have visited me in Thailand, and her father, who is like a dad to me, has been here twice.
Even though my life here is slower, I'm not one to sit still. The café gives me a sense of purpose, but I don't know if I'll ever be fully satisfied with retirement.
I took what was basically a box on the side of the road and turned it into something people seek out. I don't want 20 locations or to franchise, but now that the café is on autopilot, I'm getting bored again.
I don't think I will ever stop looking for the next thing to build. I just don't know what that'll be yet.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said President Donald Trump would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically," and prefers not to use military force.
Speaking over the weekend, Rubio told reporters that "He [Trump] hasn't made a decision...what the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it, and we really we have everything we need to be successful. But we would prefer to do it peacefully."
The remarks come as reports suggest both sides are gearing up for additional military strikes after the midterm elections.
On Saturday, Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
He also ordered that its military database be updated so that "all kinds of physical and non-physical assets of the U.S.-Zionist enemy are brought within the reach of the Armed Forces," referring to U.S. and Israeli forces.
Washington has not explicitly stated it plans to resume attacks on Iran, but reports from The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times indicate the U.S. is preparing for possible renewed military actions after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
On Sunday, Trump told the Right Side Broadcasting Network. "We've had such a victory, and we'll put it away very soon, one way or the other."
"Either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it," he added.
On Sunday, Iran's foreign ministry designated the U.K.'s Military Intelligence Services as a "hostile group" and accused the Royal Navy and Air Force of supporting "terrorist organizations." In a Telegram post , the ministry said that the move was a response to what it called London's "malicious" actions, including the designation of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as a "terrorist organization."
Tehran has separately accused the U.K. of participating in the U.S.-Iran war by allowing American forces access to British military and logistical bases.
The U.K. had allowed U.S. forces to use RAF Fairford and Diego Garcia for what were described as "defensive" strikes on Iran, according to the BBC.

Russia and Ukraine completed a remarkably successful humanitarian mission in occupied Kherson Oblast, as some Ukrainian civilians returned to Ukrainian-controlled territory. Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets noted that the Oleshky ceasefire is the longest localized ceasefire that both sides have observed since 2022.[1] Lubinets and Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova reported on October 30 and 31 that some residents of occupied Kherson Oblast, particularly from Oleshky, returned to Ukrainian-controlled territory, while others chose to stay in the area or travelled to occupied Simferopol, Crimea.[2] Ukrainian officials reported on October 31 that residents of Oleshky and nearby settlements flew to Belarus and then crossed the border into Chernihiv Oblast.[3] This humanitarian mission was remarkable in that Lubinets traveled to occupied Oleshky and Russia then back to Ukraine, Oleshky residents received humanitarian aid, and at least some civilians successfully evacuated to Ukrainian-controlled areas. The exact number of Oleshky residents who were able to leave the settlement and return to Ukrainian-controlled territory remains unclear as of this writing. ISW will provide further details on this humanitarian operation in the forthcoming Russian Occupation Update.
Both Russian and Ukrainian forces appear to have largely abided by the terms of the localized ceasefire in occupied Kherson Oblast since it came into effect on the morning of October 27, although there are limited allegations of ceasefire violations. Ukrainian Southern Group of Forces Spokesperson Maksym Kravchuk reported on October 31 that Russian forces repeatedly violated the terms of the ceasefire, including by using reconnaissance drones and dropping explosives from drones on Ukrainian positions.[4] Russian Ambassador-at-Large and former Russian occupation official Rodion Miroshnik claimed on October 31 that Ukrainian forces struck a civilian vehicle with a drone on the outskirts of Oleshky on October 31.[5] ISW is unable to independently verify these claimed ceasefire violations, but it appears that the humanitarian mission was nonetheless largely successful.
Kravchuk also noted on October 31 that Russian forces are taking advantage of the localized ceasefire in Oleshky to conduct personnel rotations, strengthen their positions and logistics, evacuate wounded and killed servicemembers, and install protection against Ukrainian drones on roads in the area.[6]
The Kremlin is refusing to compromise on its original maximalist demands from 2022 while continuing to ignore Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s offers of large-scale frontline ceasefires as Russia’s losses grow disproportionately to its territorial gains. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov on October 30 told reporters at the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting that Russia’s position on a peace settlement in Ukraine is well-known and has remained unchanged since the start of the full-scale invasion.[7] Lavrov reiterated Russia’s claimed “root causes” of the war, including the alleged discrimination against ethnic Russians and the Russian language and the spread of neo-Nazism in Ukraine. Kremlin officials have repeatedly reaffirmed their maximalist objectives throughout the war while refusing Ukrainian- and US-proposed temporary ceasefires and compromises. Ukraine and the United States first proposed an immediate 30-day ceasefire along the entire frontline on March 11, 2025.[8] The Kremlin rejected that and subsequent proposed ceasefires, and Russian forces have suffered at least 698,000 casualties and gained just over 4,000 square kilometers (about the total area of Rhode Island) since then.[9]
The Kremlin is attempting to portray Ukrainian long-range strikes against Russia as the obstacle to peace talks — the latest Russian effort to falsely blame Ukraine for Russia’s refusal to meaningfully engage in negotiations. Lavrov complained on October 30 about Ukraine’s long-range strikes deep into the Russian rear and claimed that these strikes do not signal that Ukraine is preparing for negotiations.[10] Lavrov’s statement ignores Russia’s own daily long-range strike campaigns against Ukraine and the Kremlin’s repeated rejections of US- and Ukrainian-proposed moratoriums on long-range strikes against energy infrastructure.[11] The Kremlin has used Ukrainian strikes — real and alleged — to deflect blame away from Russia for stalled peace negotiations, including after the claimed strike against Russian President Vladimir Putin’s residence in Novgorod Oblast in December 2025 and the strike against occupied Khorly, Kherson Oblast in January 2026.[12]
The Kremlin continues to try to push European leaders out of peace talks, despite Russian demands that a peace settlement restructure the European security architecture. Lavrov claimed that Europeans are trying to “squeeze” into the negotiating process and questioned the value European representatives could bring to the talks.[13] The Kremlin has recently renewed its public demands that NATO roll back to its 1997 borders – a demand that the Kremlin first issued in 2021 before the start of the full-scale invasion.[14] The Kremlin has nonetheless repeatedly demanded in recent days that European leaders not participate in talks to end the war.[15] Russian efforts to keep European representatives out of peace talks also directly contradict US President Donald Trump’s initiative for Europe to take on increased responsibility for European affairs, including European defenses and support for Ukraine.
The US Department of State approved the possible sale of 500 PAC-3 Patriot ballistic missile interceptors to Ukraine, but the delivery will reportedly not occur for several years. [16] Various Western outlets, citing unidentified sources, reported that the approval is for the delivery of newly manufactured interceptors, which is not expected until after 2030.[17] The sale therefore will not support Ukraine’s efforts to defend itself during the expected intense Russian ballistic missile strike campaign in Winter 2026-2027. Ukraine’s vulnerability resulting from insufficient ballistic missile interceptor supplies will encourage Russian President Vladimir Putin to pursue his current theory of victory that aims to use ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones to force a Ukrainian surrender through a decisive long-range strike campaign over this coming winter.[18]

Ukrainian forces struck a Russian defense industrial facility in Rostov Oblast on the night of October 30 to 31. Total sales for Wuxia action RPG Phantom Blade Zero have surpassed four million units in just 72 hours, developer S-GAME announced .
Phantom Blade Zero launched digitally for PlayStation 5 and PC via Steam and Epic Games Store on October 29. A physical edition is due out for PlayStation 5 in 2027.
Here is an overview of the game, via S-GAME:
S-GAME presents Phantom Blade Zero , a fusion of classic Wuxia storytelling and exhilarating action powered by Unreal Engine 5. You play as Soul, a warrior with only sixty-six days left to live. Fend off assassins, unravel world-ending conspiracies, and defend your values with your life.
Framed for the death of his master and left with a ruined heart, Soul has sixty-six days to live. Alone and hunted by his former comrades, he moves through a world of shifting loyalties and silent blades—determined to unravel the conspiracy that has condemned him.
Rain mixes with blood, mercy entangles with vengeance. Soul’s journey is one of love, hate, and the fragile search for what it means to have a heart.
A Masterful Blend of Traditional Wuxia, Fantasy, and Folk Horror
Explore a world beyond imagination. Shifting realities, echoes of memories long since passed, augmentation, and beings of higher power await in Phantom Blade Zero .
A rumor, a story, a whisper—every thread a trail to unraveling a larger mystery. Navigate through a web of intrigue and lies to uncover the truth.
An Extensive Arsenal is at Your Disposal
A fighter’s worth lies in their weapons.
Over thirty weapons are yours to wield, with more than twenty unique “Phantom Edges” to mix and match to suit your playstyle.
Defeat powerful foes to obtain their weapons, and with it, their signature techniques. Grow your arsenal and defeat all who stand in your path.
Inspired by the Golden Age of Hong Kong action films, the world of Phantom Blade Zero blends fierce martial arts with machinery, amplifying an exhilarating clash of steel on steel.
Ancient codes meet iron and smoke; tradition thrums to a modern beat. A new style is forged in this melding of mediums. This is Kungfupunk.
An Authentic Kungfu Experience
Built in Unreal Engine 5 and through the use of state-of-the-art motion capture, Phantom Blade Zero brings together legendary fight choreography from Hong Kong’s Golden Age of martial arts cinema.
Every strike and stance draws from authentic martial arts techniques, captured with the precision of film, is reborn through modern game design.
This is Chinese kungfu reimagined for a new generation.

articles.title_orig: King to address slavery in Antigua as PM says he is open to possible UK apology
articles.title_zh: King to address slavery in Antigua as PM says he is open to possible UK apology
articles.content_orig:
King Charles III is to speak with "unflinching honesty" and "sincere sorrow" on the lasting pain of the transatlantic slave trade during the final leg of his Caribbean tour in Antigua, Buckingham Palace has said.
The King will address Commonwealth leaders on Tuesday in a speech that will touch on the issue.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier that he was "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in slavery - a change in the government's stance.
It is understood the Palace was told in advance of Burnham's comments in an opinion piece on Friday night, and that the King has not made any changes to his speech in light of them.
The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations.
Burnham has previously stuck with the policy of his predecessors and stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments.
In an address to the nation to mark Antigua and Barbuda's independence day, Prime Minister Gaston Browne said the history of slavery was painful and "its consequences have not disappeared with the passage of time".
He said the country's pursuit of reparatory justice deserved "seriousness, sensitivity and sustained international engagement".
Browne went on to say that his government was having these conversations in bilateral discussions with the UK and other Commonwealth countries at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch described "endless talk about apologies" as a "distraction" from solving current problems.
She told BBC Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "The transatlantic slave trade happened centuries ago. It is time for the Commonwealth to start looking forwards, not endlessly backwards."
The King will make his speech at the CHOGM.
He "will not shy away from confronting the most shameful aspects of the past during this visit", a Palace spokesperson said.
"You may therefore expect him to address them in his speech with unflinching honesty, sincere sorrow and respect for the wider discussions that will be taking place between relevant governments on this issue at CHOGM and beyond."
When asked about the King's reaction to the prime minister's comments, the spokesperson said it would "not be appropriate" for the King to address matters of policy relating to the government's position.
The Caribbean tour has again thrust the King into the difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.
On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech in which he spoke of the "suffering of the past".
In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion , where hundreds of enslaved people were killed.
Buckingham Palace said it was a moment for the King to learn more about the history of slavery and resistance. His engagements have also covered the environment, opportunities for young people and trade relationships with the UK.
Royal sources have stressed that the decisions around making an apology were a matter for government, not the Palace.
"His Majesty is well practised on the diplomatic tightrope," a Royal aide said. "He is up for challenging visits with complex issues and relationships in play. He sees it as his role to bat for Britain, the Realms and wider Commonwealth."
In a piece for the Guardian published on Friday night, Burnham described the transatlantic slave trade as a "brutal and barbaric violation" , and said Britain "must face up to the past".
His separate pledge in his article to strengthen the work of the Commonwealth as an organisation will be welcomed by the King, who views the collection of 56 countries as a powerful vehicle for change.
The King will be giving the opening speech at CHOGM, which gathers leaders from those 56 states every two years in a different part of the Commonwealth.
Each biennial meeting's official theme this year is Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth.
Queen Camilla is with the King in Antigua and, as the couple attended a church service on Sunday morning ahead of joining celebrations to mark Independence Day on the island, there was a reminder of what the intended focus of the week will be.
Bishop of North Eastern Caribbean and Aruba, Ernest Flemming, told the congregation the "prosperity" of the Commonwealth must be a "shared prosperity".
"True partnership requires mutual respect, it requires listening, it requires fairness."
A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said: "Institutions are under strain across the globe. The Commonwealth has scale and breadth, but is also small enough for leaders to know each other and co-operate together."
The King, they said, "contributes ideas and encouragement on a wide range of issues, delivering practical results which help improve the lives of millions".
Later on Sunday, the King was left drenched and without an umbrella when a torrential downpour interrupted an Independence Day ceremony.
The Queen was swiftly given an umbrella when the rain started, while the King was seen gesturing to be given one of his own.
It has been a difficult few months for the King, with developments surrounding his brother, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor , and the publication of a book by his former brother-in-law, Earl Spencer.
In addition, his son, the Duke of Sussex, made a surprise move back to the UK with his wife Meghan and their two children in August.
Asked whether the King was confident that his approach to family matters had been the right one in terms of public attitudes towards the institution, the response was concise. "Yes," a senior aide told the BBC. "That is why he takes the actions he does - and has done."
On the serious allegations that have emerged about Meghan's father , Thomas Markle, the Palace did not want to get involved publicly: "We wouldn't comment on private family matters."
The King is also still being treated for cancer. He was diagnosed in early 2024 and the Palace says he remains on a "positive trajectory".
In hot and humid conditions, he will soon celebrate his 78th birthday and will have carried out about 36 engagements by the end of this nine-day tour of the Caribbean.

articles.content_orig:
Financial experts from Warren Buffett on down often urge retail investors to own a portfolio spread across the broad U.S. stock market. And if you own a fund that tracks the S&P 500, you more or less have just that — a who's who of the largest stocks available on U.S. exchanges.
But what happens when a new bombshell enters the proverbial villa?
Index fund investors may be pondering that exact question, given the news that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said he's considering a tie-up with Tesla . When SpaceX reported its third-quarter financial results last week, Musk said on the earnings call that he'd consider a combination with the Austin, Texas-based electric car maker, in what would be the largest merger in history.
What's more, on Monday, AI firm Anthropic filed an S-1 with the Securities and Exchange Commission, signaling the company's intention to go public.
Both could be huge companies. Doing a little back-of-the-napkin math, SpaceX and Tesla sport market capitalizations, calculated by multiplying share price by shares outstanding, of $2 trillion and $1.55 trillion, respectively. Smash those together, and a theoretical $3.55 trillion company would be the fifth-largest company on the market. Experts say Anthropic could seek a valuation between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion at its offering, which at current prices could make it between the world's eighth- and twelfth-largest firm.
But if you hold an S&P 500 fund, that doesn't necessarily mean you're about to have new top-10 holdings. Here's why, and why index mechanics matter for your portfolio.
It's easy to think of the S&P 500 as a very straightforward, math-based index. If you assumed the index merely held the 500 largest stocks on the market, weighted by market size, you'd be mostly right.
But if you're already invested in an S&P 500 fund — and many people are; S&P Dow Jones Indices estimated about $16 trillion was invested in products designed to track the S&P 500 as of year-end 2025 — you may have noticed that SpaceX isn't included in the portfolio. That's because S&P generally has a 12-month waiting period for newly public stocks to join the index, meaning that Musk's rocket firm will have to wait until June 2027 to be considered for inclusion.
Anthropic could face a similar waiting period before S&P's index committee considers the stock for admission.
As for a potential Musk-led supercompany, experts say its inclusion and weighting in the index would come down to several factors, including the mechanics of the merger and the percentage of shares of the combined company made available to the public.
A representative from S&P Dow Jones Indices told CNBC Make It that the firm does not comment on hypothetical scenarios or any company's eligibility for index inclusion. The firm's methodology states that each merger and acquisition is reviewed on a case-by-base basis. If an acquiring company is in the S&P 500 and acquires a firm not in the index, that firm generally stays in the index, though S&P could remove it if the transaction affects its eligibility. Non-members that acquire members can be added, too, provided they meet other eligibility criteria, at the index committee's discretion.
It remains to be seen if and when Anthropic or a Tesla/SpaceX combo would be added to the S&P 500. But if they eventually make it into an index fund you own, experts say there are a couple of key things to consider.
One would be a bump in exposure to Musk-led firms, meaning that more of your portfolio could be tied to the tech CEO's vision of the future, says Seth Goldstein, a senior equity analyst at investment research firm Morningstar.
"For direct holders of Tesla or SpaceX, you're holding the stock because you believe in Elon Musk's vision and believe that he can turn seemingly conceptual products into a reality," Goldstein says. "Whether that is cars that can drive themselves [or] humanoid robots that can be useful, he has these sort of grand visions for future technologies, and he has the ability to bring them into real products."
Another consideration is concentration risk — the idea that much of the fate of a particular portfolio is tied to a small number of investments. Nearly 40% of assets in any given S&P 500 fund are currently invested in the index's top-10 holdings, many of which are directly or tangentially tied to the proliferation of artificial intelligence. From December 1965 through March 2026, the S&P 500's top-10 constituents accounted for 23% of the index, on average, according to research from T. Rowe Price .
Additions of a SpaceX/Tesla firm or of Anthropic could further tilt the S&P 500 toward tech and AI, and, more broadly, toward companies whose stocks have already seen major run-ups, says Brent Leadbetter, head of RAFI distribution at investment research firm TMX VettaFi.
"We are wary of concentration. By definition, the shares of firms that reach the top of cap-weighted indices have appreciated at a faster rate than the firms they have surpassed," Leadbetter says. "These recent winners are often expensive as a result. Investing in expensive companies is too often a way for investors to chase strong past returns only to realize modest future returns."

articles.content_orig:
After debuting the refreshed iPad mini with OLED this past week, Apple still has more in the pipeline for the rest of the iPad lineup in the first half of next year. That includes a new iPad Air , a new base iPad , and a new iPad Pro , according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman .
To follow up the iPad mini refresh, Apple’s next iPad Air refresh will also gain OLED. It’ll likely stick with a 60Hz panel, and likely won’t make the switch from Touch ID to Face ID – but it’ll bring a nifty display upgrade to the iPad Air , a product that hasn’t had a major refresh since 2020.
In terms of chipset, while not confirmed, a jump from the M4 chip to the M5 chip is rather likely. It’ll also likely come with a higher price, likely around $799-899 for the base 11-inch model.
Next year, Apple will also finally update the base iPad for the first time since early 2025. It’ll upgrade it to the A19 chip and 8GB of RAM, finally enabling Apple Intelligence support on Apple’s cheapest iPad. It should also gain the N1 chip and the C1X modem for improved networking performance.
There shouldn’t be any screen or design upgrades with this iPad , at least as of now – though it could potentially see some refreshed color options.
Really makes wonder whether Apple even has a place & purpose for the iPad anymore - with the launch of touchscreen MacBooks, iPhone that opens into an iPad, iPad that serves as a home hub control with stand, and iPhone chips that now run macOS.
With the iPad Pro , Apple will be adding a vapor chamber to the device, a feat it started last year with the iPhone 17 Pro. It probably won’t have any meaningful changes otherwise, except for a new chipset – likely M6 or potentially M7.
Hopefully, there’s some surprises in store with this device. The iPad Pro now starts at $1199 for an 11-inch model and $1499 for a 13-inch model. It’ll have been around 3 years since the last major revamp by the time Apple introduces the M6 model, and the company should probably do something to make it a more worthwhile refresh.

articles.title_orig: GDPx: Measuring Frontier Model Capabilities Across the Most Valuable Domains
articles.title_zh: GDPx: Measuring Frontier Model Capabilities Across the Most Valuable Domains
articles.content_orig:
GDPx is a benchmark that covers the most valuable domains for frontier intelligence. It aims to be the world’s best benchmark for measuring general agentic capabilities.
We believe the first trillion dollars of AI revenue will be concentrated in sectors that can deploy frontier intelligence at high ROI , not broadly diffused throughout the whole economy. Building a general-purpose benchmark based on share of GDP or the SOC/O*NET occupational taxonomy is therefore a mistake. If your goal is to track the progress of frontier models, you should focus on the domains where they will be most impactful.
Specifically, we cover the following domains:
Recursive self-improvement (RSI)
And intentionally forgo industries like government, real estate, and insurance.
GDPx is a true frontier-level benchmark: even the best model scores just 12%.
It’s worth emphasizing that certain models like Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra have sandbagged overall scores due to their safety classifiers. If we exclude cyber, biology, and alignment—the three domains where safety classifiers sometimes kick in—you get the following results instead.
We were pleasantly surprised by how well this ranking lines up with our subjective impression of the models. OpenAI and Anthropic generally dominate the top of the ranking while SpaceXAI, Meta, and open-weight models are all meaningfully behind. Gemini 4 Carbon is a real improvement from Google and the only model in the same ballpark as Opus and Astra. It will be interesting to see people’s impressions once Carbon becomes generally available.
We believe it’s underrated how relevant safety classifiers are when picking the best model for certain use cases. For example, Muse Wonder Full is actually the best available cyber model today by a meaningful margin .
We also generally observe meaningful spikiness across all leading models.
Opus 5.5 is the best all-around model and wins in quant trading, hardware design, and chip design. Gemini 4 Carbon is the best bio model (likely due to weaker safety classifiers) and edges out the win in software engineering. GPT-6 Astra wins convincingly for RSI and is also the best model for materials science. Our finance and legal tasks are so challenging that basically every model scores exactly 0.
Interestingly, if you subset to a single model family, you will sometimes see very similar spikes.
The cost vs performance Pareto frontier also matches our general experience using the models: Luna and DeepSeek fight for the low end, Opus wins the high end, and OpenAI claims the middle. Again, however, the appearance of Gemini 4 Carbon is worth watching closely.
It’s impossible to make all the nuanced comparisons enabled by GDPx in a single newsletter. To explore the data yourself, checkout the official website .
Domain-specific benchmarks have gotten significantly better over the past year largely thanks to the rise of specialized RL environment startups. Yet OpenAI’s GDPval (along with its derivatives like GDPval AA v2.1 ) remains the most popular general purpose benchmark still reported on major new model release cards . This is despite being released over a year ago on September 25, 2025—an eternity in AI land. GDPval may have been marketed as a “knowledge work” benchmark, but agents weren’t really even a thing yet. This had a huge impact on its task design, and as we’ll later explain, makes GDPval woefully inadequate for evaluating today’s frontier models.
Our goal with GDPx is to create the world’s best benchmark for general agentic capabilities. However, as soon as we started working on this project, it became clear why we’ve yet to see a worthy GDPval successor. Models like GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5 are already pushing the boundaries of human knowledge. If you want to make a finance or cyber task these models can only solve < 20% of the time, you need real domain expertise to ensure the task is hard for the right reasons. Many popular benchmarks sidestep this problem by shipping tasks that are downright unfair . This typically manifests in a grader that checks for requirements impossible to infer from the task description or environment. For example, a coding problem may ask the model to fix a bug that a human engineer would agree has two valid solutions—one using “module A” and another using “module B”. However, a poorly designed grader may require the AI to use “module A” and unfairly give 0 reward when the AI chooses “module B”. Correct all such issues, and the benchmark often ends up being saturated .
Making high quality tasks for a single domain you have expertise in is already hard enough—there’s a reason why labs are willing to pay $5k+ for a single high quality task. Finding one company with sufficient expertise in both AI evals and enough domains to make a broad-based GDP benchmark is downright impossible.
To solve this problem, SemiAnalysis partnered with specialized RL environment startups for each domain:
Chip Design ( Aria , Arcverex , Ergodex )
Cybersecurity ( Arithmetic )
Finance ( Living Context )
Quant trading ( Third Moment )
Hardware design ( Beautiful Machines )
Materials science ( ValenceForge , Emulated )
Software engineering ( Datacurve )
All partners were subject to a rigorous QA process we detail in the methodology section. For some domains, we had multiple partners who wanted to be exclusive and ran a process to select the one with the highest quality tasks.
We would like to give a huge thank you to all of our partners for contributing to GDPx. They’re among the best vendors for their respective domains and it would’ve been impossible to create such a broad-based benchmark without their help.
Additionally, we’d like to thank Fireworks for providing inference for all the open source models, Modal for providing the sandbox infra needed to run our tasks, as well as Abhijay Rana for helping source some of the partners and assisting with early QA.
To be clear, we believe GDPval was impressive for its time and was the first benchmark to evaluate AI on such a broad range of tasks. It’s not OpenAI’s fault that a benchmark created before the rise of agents does a poor job evaluating them today.
Every GDPval task is precisely specified and non-interactive, with all the necessary context directly spoon-fed to the model in the prompt. Consider the following representative finance example below:
Attached to this prompt is a very plain, single-page PDF that gives the model even more context about the two projects.
From here, the model is asked to directly one-shot its task of writing a 15 page pdf to recommend one of the two options.
Any real finance manager could point out dozens of reasons why this task isn’t actually representative of their day to day work, but we will focus on two main issues:
Despite the task description itself being unnaturally wordy, the overall task lacks detail about the “two significant investment opportunities.” The model is expected to take nothing more than a ~500 word, high-level description of the two options and convert it into an “up to 15 page” pdf recommending one of them. As you’d expect, even OpenAI’s reference solution is mostly filler slop.
Relatedly, the task simply lacks a realistic, rich environment. A human expert tasked with making a recommendation between two investment opportunities would do a ton of research first to gather information—searching through pdfs, excel models, emails, etc. This process of gathering context is a big part of what makes actual work difficult and is entirely missing from GDPval.
This second point is extremely important to understand. Not including domain-specific, simulated work environments for each task is the single biggest issue with GDPval. Agents today have already progressed well beyond narrow, well-scoped tasks like “generate a pdf/excel file/word doc/powerpoint based on just this reference file attached below + a few hundred word prompt,” yet basically every GDPval task fits this exact shape. articles.title_orig: Ukraine air raid app apparently hacked as users receive false radiation threat, Air Force says
articles.title_zh: Ukraine air raid app apparently hacked as users receive false radiation threat, Air Force says
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine's air raid alert app was apparently hacked on Sunday and for a short time said the capital Kyiv was subject to a radiation threat, the Ukrainian Air Force has said.
The alert on Telegram read: "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel."
The Ukrainian Central Intelligence Agency said there had been a failure in the app, and urged people to use other sources of information to clarify the situation on the threat of air strikes.
A few hours later Russian authorities said its app was hacked. A Ukrainian espionage group claimed fake warnings of nuclear strikes inside Russia had been sent to users.
Russia has the world's biggest nuclear arsenal, and President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly suggested an openness to using all weapons at Russia's disposal .
The alerts, in Ukrainian, started at approximately 22:47 (20:47 GMT), with red-level air raids apparently issued nationwide. Additional warnings were issued in Kyiv, with the first reading: "Radiation threat.  Radiation threat declared in Kyiv."
The next message, written in Russian, came at 22:48, which read: "Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don't worry, it's Oreshnik flying".
A third alert, at 22:49, again in Ukrainian, said "Chemical threat. There is a threat of a chemical attack on Kyiv. Don't go outside."
At 22:49, a fourth alert stated there was a "Street fighting threat. Street fighting is taking place in Kyiv. Don't go outside."
At 23:53 a series of all clear messages were then delivered to users' phones, which were connected to each of the previous Kyiv alerts, individually declaring each threat clear.
In a separate post on Telegram, the Ukrainian Central Intelligence Agency said that due to the Air Alert application, the Radiation Hazard signal was played on loudspeaker devices in the Lviv region, and added there was no threat of radiation hazard.
If the alert app is not working, Ukraine's Centre for Countering Disinformation advises the public to turn on notifications on their smartphones, pay attention to sirens, and to only read official sources
Several leaders of other regions also posted on Telegram that the app had apparently been hacked and there was no local threat.
"Everything is calm in the region for now," said Svitlana Onyshchuk, the governor of the Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast. The app had reported a red-level air raid alert for the oblast in Ukraine's east, between 22:50 and 23:57.
The Vinnytsia regional head, Natalya Zabolotna, said there had been a cyber-attack on the Air Alert app and posted a warning on Telegram not to click on the link in the message, which could be a phishing attempt.
The Air Alert app is supported by the Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine, and informs users instantly about the beginning and end of defence alerts. The ministry had earlier said the app was temporarily disabled for maintenance after it had "apparently been compromised". It urged residents to turn on their smartphones' emergency notifications so they could receive state-issued distress signals.
A few hours after the false alerts in Ukraine, Russia's ministry of emergency situations said its app had been subjected to "a massive cyberattack" which sent "fake information to the public".
No further details were given by the ministry or state media.
Ukrainian news outlet, UNN, reported the hack sent fake alerts of a nuclear threat inside Russia.
Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian held territory, said on its Telegram page that the app had been hacked, accompanied with laughing emojis.
A screenshot of a purported emergency alert published by Atesh, which has not been verified by the BBC, told users to "urgently" stock up on provisions for three weeks and take cover in basements. It also used obscene language. Atesh has been contacted for comment.
The alerts occurred just minutes before the end of a localised ceasefire in Ukraine's front-line Kherson region , which was implemented last Tuesday and officially ended at 23:00 Sunday.
Fighting had continued elsewhere while the Kherson ceasefire was in place, to allow civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky .
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

articles.title_zh: Binance sees $3.64 billion in net outflows as withdrawals resume after massive hack
articles.content_orig:
Binance said it recorded $3.64 billion in net outflows after reopening withdrawals on Sunday following a $6.3 billion hack, as customers rushed to move funds off the platform.
The exchange processed $4.65 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits between 6 a.m. and 3:30 p.m. UTC on Nov. 1, Binance said in a post on X.
The resulting net outflows represented 2.1% of Binance's $171 billion in total assets, based on its latest available proof-of-reserves data as of Oct. 28.
Binance said withdrawal volumes had declined and were stabilizing following an initial spike, while deposit volumes remained substantial.
The exchange began restoring withdrawals in phases at 6 a.m. UTC on Sunday, with services resuming across all 15 networks and assets included in the initial phase by 12:36 p.m. UTC. It said testing was continuing for the remaining networks and assets.
Binance founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao sought to reassure users following the breach, writing on X that "98% choose to stay!" He said most of the net outflows occurred within the first couple of hours after withdrawals resumed. "Trust isn't earned by what you say in good times. It's earned by what you do in hard times," Zhao added.
The withdrawals followed a record $6.3 billion hack of Binance last week. The FBI attributed the attack to North Korean hackers, identifying the operation as TraderTraitor.
The exchange has said it would absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds rather than pass the losses on to users.
Binance said it had covered around 95% of the impacted amount, up from 90% in its previous update. The exchange said the remaining 5% consisted of less liquid tokens that would take longer to source in the quantities required.

A Marib-based Yemeni journalist reported that Houthi fighters advanced onto elevated terrain in al Maqatirah District, Lahij Governorate, on November 1.[2] Pro-Yemeni government media reported that Yemeni government reinforcements deployed to the district later on November 1.[3] The source did not specify whether Yemeni government-aligned forces recaptured territory in al Maqatirah District, which suggests that the area remains contested at the time of this writing.[4] Yemeni government-aligned forces reportedly repelled another Houthi attempt to advance southeastward from southern Taiz Governorate into al Maqatirah District on October 30. The Houthis likely seek to capture terrain that overlooks Tur al Balah District and leads to Aden City. Such territory would support a potential Houthi effort to besiege or capture Aden City.[5]
Yemeni government-aligned forces continued to engage Houthi fighters in central Jawf Governorate on November 1. A Marib-based Yemeni journalist reported that Yemeni government-aligned forces repelled a Houthi attempt to advance to Jabal Huwayshiyan from the northeast. Jabal Huwayshiyan is a mountain range overlooking al Hazm, the governorate’s capital.[6] Yemeni government-aligned forces recaptured Jabal Huwayshiyan between October 30 and 31.[7] Yemeni government-aligned forces are likely attempting to recapture territory in central Jawf Governorate as part of an effort to set conditions to recapture al Hazm.[8]

Saudi air defenses intercepted one Houthi ballistic missile and one drone launched toward Saudi Arabia’s southern region on November 1. [13] The Houthis have not claimed the attack as of this writing. The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Saudi critical infrastructure as part of the Houthis’ ongoing strike campaign to compel Saudi Arabia to halt military operations against the Houthis and accept the Houthis’ demands, which include lifting Saudi controls on Houthi-controlled ports and airports and granting the Houthis control over Yemen’s oil and gas resources.[14]

articles.content_orig:
Good evening. If all had gone according to plan, the United States v Wanzhou Meng and Huawei Technologies would have opened in a federal courtroom in the waning months of President Donald Trump’s first term. And what a trial it would have been: an heir to one of China’s most successful and strategically important companies, detained in Canada and extradited to the U.S., on trial for allegedly lying to banks about Huawei operations in Iran that were in violation of American sanctions on the country. But Xi Jinping forestalled that humiliating spectacle by ordering the arrest of two Canadians in China, Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor, and not releasing them until the U.S. and Canada allowed Meng, the daughter of Huawei’s founder, to return to China in September 2021. Five years later the United States v Huawei Technologies , minus Meng, is finally underway. Noah Berman reports from the courtroom in Brooklyn.
In other articles, Leon Panetta speaks with Bob Davis about his dealings with China as a Congressman, White House Chief-of-Staff, CIA Director and Secretary of Defense.
Noah Berman on DayOne , the Singaporean data center operator that is helping Chinese companies realise their AI ambitions.
In The Big Picture , Savannah Billman writes about the enormous popularity of AI-generated “short dramas” in China.
Lizzi C. Lee and Simon Hedlin on the barriers to a common-sense Sino-U.S. AI safety agreement .
And finally, be sure to catch up on the latest episode of our weekly podcast , with Peiyue Wu talking about her recent cover on dual-use farms in China.
Want this emailed directly to your inbox? Sign up to receive our free newsletter.
In 2021 Meng Wanzhou, daughter of Huawei Technologies founder Ren Zhengfei, signed a “statement of facts” to resolve U.S. charges against her. According to that statement, “Ms. Meng [told HSBC] … Huawei’s relationship with Skycom was ‘normal business cooperation’ and … she described Skycom as a … ‘third party Huawei works with’ in Iran … Those statements were untrue because, as Ms. Meng knew, … Huawei controlled Skycom.” The U.S. let Meng go regardless because the Chinese government made it clear that it would not release two Canadian hostages until she was freed. Five years later the U.S. government’s case against Huawei is finally underway in New York, with Meng safely back in China.
Leon Panetta fought with, and engaged with China over a long career in politics. The former Congressman, White House Chief of Staff, CIA Director and Defense Secretary talks with Bob Davis about why China thinks President Trump is good for China.
“If China senses weakness, they’ll take advantage of it,” Panetta says. “Right now, China is in a stronger position because we’re locked in a war in Iran, our economy is being impacted by that war, and there’s a lot of unpredictability about the U.S. China has been able to take advantage in areas where once we had some influence, particularly in the Pacific.”
Illustration by Lauren Crow
The U.S. government doesn’t want America’s best chips to power Chinese data centers that would then help Chinese companies hone their AI models and applications. DayOne, a Singapore-based data center provider, profits from this by building data centers in Southeast Asia where Chinese AI firms can legally access America’s best chips. Noah Berman looks at DayOne and the IPO prospectus it has just issued. “DayOne’s rise,” he writes, “illustrates how companies can profit, and even gain backing from American investors, as U.S. export controls lead Chinese companies to seek access to data centers overseas.”
Are you, like the Old Dad who writes this newsletter, also a parent who dreads the short videos on YouTube and elsewhere that so easily reel in your kids? Alas, writes Savannah Billman , if China is anything to go by — as it increasingly is when it comes to tech trends — the madness is only going to get worse. Almost 900 million (!) Chinese people are watching AI-generated “short dramas”, issued as a seemingly endless stream of two-minute videos, on a new generation of apps tailored to the new genre. Over the first half of this year alone about 267,000 AI short videos were released. Ugh.
Recent steps taken towards the establishment of a U.S.-China AI incident-reporting channel are important, write Lizzi C. Lee and Simon Hedlin . But, they add, there is “a more pressing issue: frontier AI companies currently do not provide the information they need”.

articles.title_zh: Iran’s top diplomat hopes US shows ‘rationality,’ and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
“Some progress” has been made in efforts to reach an agreement between the US and Iran, several sources familiar with the negotiations told The Jerusalem Post . However, the sources stressed that "significant gaps remain between the two sides".
“There is some optimism that an agreement can be reached. But there is still work to be done,” one source said.
Another source said no progress had been made on the nuclear issue and that the advances concerned other matters, including the timeline for implementing a potential agreement.
In recent days, Qatari mediators have intensified indirect diplomatic efforts between the US and Iran amid growing fears of a potential military escalation following the US midterm elections.
An Iranian delegation traveled to Doha for several days of talks, coordinated closely with Washington, following intensive consultations in Tehran. The discussions reportedly focus on proposals to de-escalate the eight-month-old conflict, including a potential two-day framework for reopening the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz and resuming broader peace negotiations.
Despite these diplomatic efforts, significant gaps remain between the two sides. Tehran is demanding that Washington lift recent sanctions, reinstate oil waivers, reduce its regional military presence, and end port blockades before addressing restrictions on Iran's nuclear program.
By contrast, US officials, following recent outreach by Vice President JD Vance to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei , insist that any comprehensive agreement must address nuclear concerns from the outset.
On Sunday, US President Donald Trump was asked how negotiations with Iran were progressing.
“They're going fine, but they're not very reliable. They make a deal and then they back out,” he responded.
Trump also said there were “one or two sites” in Iran's nuclear program that the US needed to address.
“But we can do that in 10 minutes,” he added.
A source familiar with the matter confirmed to the Post that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Trump spoke by phone on Saturday. The call came days after Trump was briefed by US Central Command (CENTCOM) commander Adm. Brad Cooper on military options for a possible operation against Iran.
Meanwhile, Iranian Deputy Parliament Speaker Ali Nikzad said Iran had no intention of negotiating over its nuclear program, regardless of the pressure exerted on it.
Dr. Raz Zimmt, head of the Iran and Shi'ite Axis Research Program at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), told The Jerusalem Post that each side currently needs something from the other that cannot be reversed, while neither is willing to make what would constitute an irreversible concession.
“The Americans are prepared to lift the naval blockade and some of the sanctions, since these measures can be reinstated, and in return they are demanding something on the nuclear front, such as an inspectors' visit and/or action regarding the enriched uranium. The Iranians, meanwhile, are prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and perhaps even allow inspectors to visit certain sites, but they are unwilling to give up their enriched uranium. Instead, they are demanding something permanent, such as the unfreezing of Iranian assets.
“I find it difficult to see how this deadlock can be resolved,” Zimmt said.
Nevertheless, he added that, given the risks of another round of military confrontation, he would not rule out the possibility that the two sides could ultimately reach a compromise, even if only a temporary one.
